Leah · Genesis 29:30-35

God is Near to the Broken-hearted

From The God Who Hears Her by Dr. Connie Champeon · 3 min read

““He [Jacob] went in also to Rachel, and he loved also Rachel more than Leah, and served with him seven more years. The LORD saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren. Leah conceived, and bore a son, and she named him Reuben. For she said, “Because the LORD has looked at my affliction; for now my husband will love me.” She conceived again, and bore a son, and said, “Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has therefore given me this son also.” She named him Simeon. She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Levi. She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing.” (Genesis 29:30-35)

There is a gold thread that runs through the Scripture. It is the theme of “El Roi,” the God who sees, seeing His daughters in their desperation and isolation. God is not only found in holy or perfect places. That is really good because there aren’t many of those places around. My God is most often found with those who are unloved, whose hearts are broken and spirits crushed. The struggle is when I am the one unloved and crushed it is hard for me to realize He is there.

“The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.” (Psalm 34:18)

“Hated” in Genesis 29:31 is a technical, legal term in the Ancient Near East. It conveys Leah’s legal status not just an emotion. Even though she was the first wife, Jacob did not treat her as his primary spouse. He had officially withdrawn his preference. He loved Rachel as a first wife, and in comparison, Leah was the unloved one. On its own the word translated “hated” is very strong. However, in the context, because it is talking about how much Jacob loved Rachel, it is used to show a contrast. In other words, compared to his love for Rachel he hated Leah.

This is one of sixty devotions through the women of Genesis.

God gave Leah the thing most valued by women in the ANE - sons, many sons. Her sons' names chronicle her journey.

Reuben “See, a son!” - "The Lord has seen my misery. Surely my husband will love me now." Simeon “Hearing” - "Because the Lord heard that I am not loved, he gave me this one too." Levi “attached” - "Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." Judah “Praise” - "This time I will praise the Lord."

Leah didn’t want to be the first wife in name only. She deeply longed for Jacob’s heart. I do not know how Leah endured this transactional intimacy without losing her soul, but somehow through this struggle she found God. For 6-7 years she struggled to have Jacob see her as something other than Laban’s deception. Jacob fulfilled his legal obligation to her, but that is all. She kept dreaming that giving him sons would make him care for her as a first wife, but that never seemed to happen while Rachel was alive. But God gave Leah the Covenant seed; through her son Levi, the priestly line and through Judah, the royal line that leads to Christ.

Finally, through her naming of her sons we watch Leah’s focus shift. Reuben, Simeon, Levi — every name is a plea for Jacob to see her, hear her, attach to her. But with Judah, something breaks open. She stops naming her sons after what she wants from Jacob and simply says, 'This time I will praise the Lord.' Until that moment, she is a victim of neglect — seeking validation from a man who will never give it. With Judah she finds her sufficiency, her 'enoughness' in God. While Jacob is lusting after Rachel, God is building a Kingdom through Leah.

I struggle when I am working hard in a system that doesn’t see my value. There are many equivalents to the “beautiful favorite.” Many of us have worked in situations where there is a new “golden boy” every couple years while our hard work and dedication seems to pass relatively unnoticed. It’s easy for me to seek my value in my output instead of in God. It is easy for feeling unseen to turn to heartache and a crushed spirit. I have to remind myself that I am loved with a steadfast, loyal love by the God who sees. He sees my heartache, my exhaustion, my disappointment. When I praise Him in the midst of it all, everything shifts, and my dejection becomes a victory dance with arms lifted to heaven.
